description: Swinging Monkeys! A high-energy squad made up of three fearless 10-to-12-year-olds and two dads just trying to keep up. Powered by endless kid stamina, dad jokes, and a love for the game, we’re here to swing for the fences, have a blast, and show everyone how teamwork across generations is done.
summary: Supply Run to Bravo is a game that helps junior astronauts train for a mission to Mars. It is designed for children aged 9 to 12. The goal is to drive a rover across the planet and deliver food to the Bravo base, facing the real dangers of a Mars mission in a fun, kid-friendly setting: limited power and oxygen, solar radiation, and communication failures. To survive, players must read critical mission data, design the right rover before setting out, navigate through storms, and take action to complete the mission by delivering the supplies successfully. Fun and engagement were at the heart of the design. The game offers a blocky world to explore and multiplayer missions that make learning social and competitive, preparing young future astronauts through play.
details:
Base Alpha on Mars is shutting down, and its food has to reach Base Bravo, 24 km away. The player (aged 9 to 12) and a crewmate design a rover, load it, and drive the food across rocky plains, dunes, a crater rim, a lava tube and an icy lowland. On the way they meet the real dangers of a Mars mission: limited power and oxygen, dust storms, solar radiation and communication failures. No setting is "always best". Every choice helps one system and hurts another, so players learn the way mission planners do: by weighing trade-offs with real numbers.

The mission flow

  1. Choose a mode. Solo (Easy, Medium or Hard) or Multiplayer (Medium or Hard, up to 5 astronauts per lobby).
  2. Fly to Mars (optional mini-game). Drop rocket stages when their fuel reaches the green zone, steer the 203-day cruise past micrometeoroids, shelter from a flare, then land. The flight numbers come from Perseverance (launched 30 July 2020, landed 18 February 2021).
  3. Design the rover in the garage. Pick a frame, wheels, suspension, motors, power source and hull. The whole rover must stay under the 2,300 kg launch limit.
  4. Load up at Base Alpha. Fill the cargo rack with food crates and supplies.
  5. Drive 24 km to Bravo. Survive the hazards, then park beside the dome to unload.
  6. Repeat until all the food is delivered. Each base refills oxygen and repairs. The mission time goes on a world leaderboard, and badges reward good choices.

Time runs at 1 real second = 1 mission minute. One drive takes about 2.5 mission hours, which is a few real minutes.

The key metrics kids trade off

Each metric appears on a gauge on screen and is tied to a real number (see section 5).

Power (battery and solar panels)

  • Use: life support takes 0.7 kW all the time, the cargo heater 0.5 kW, and driving about 4 to 9 kW depending on speed, hills and rover mass.
  • Supply: solar panels give at most about 2 kW at noon with clean panels and clear skies. Night, the lava tube or a deep dust storm brings that to zero. Sunlight at Mars is set at about 590 W/m², 43% of Earth's.
  • The choice: a big solar array (120 kg, 28 kWh battery) is light but useless in the dark. A big battery pack (260 kg) stores 46 kWh. A mini fission reactor (420 kg) gives about 1 kW day and night, but it is heavy and comes with a small battery.
  • What happens at zero: the rover can't drive and the heaters switch off until the sun recharges it.

Life support (oxygen)

  • Use: two astronauts breathe 0.84 kg of oxygen each per day (NASA's BVAD planning number), about 0.07 kg an hour.
  • The choice: the rover starts with about 3.6 hours of air. Each oxygen tank adds about 5 hours but weighs 14 kg, taking cargo space that could carry food. Going outside (EVA) uses oxygen 1.5 times faster, and a damaged hull leaks air.
  • What happens at zero: the mission is lost. This is the one hard fail state.

Radiation (shielding)

  • Normal dose: about 0.67 mSv per day on the surface (0.03 mSv/h), as measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument.
  • Solar flares (five real flares from 2017 and 2024) push the dose to about 14 mSv/h in the open, and they also cause electronics faults.
  • The choice: stop and press F for shelter and safe mode (half the dose, about 10 times fewer faults), drive to the lava tube (blocks about 97%), or build a thick roof, where ice blocks count double. Water-jacket walls cut the dose further but weigh 200 kg.
  • Score: finishing with a crew dose under 5 mSv earns the "Radiation Safe" badge. NASA's 600 mSv career limit is shown for context.

Communication

  • Radio signals take 3 to 22 minutes between Earth and Mars, so nobody can drive for you. Mission Control still sends storm warnings, flare alerts and real-data facts.
  • The choice: a flare can cause a radio fault, and every message turns to static. Fixing it means going outside, which costs oxygen. Skipping the fix saves air but means driving blind into the next storm.

Mass budget (the trade-off that links them all)

  • The rover must launch under 2,300 kg. The heaviest parts are the power source and the shielding, so players can rarely have the best of both.
  • A heavier rover also needs more power to drive.
  • The default balanced rover weighs 1,810 kg, which leaves room for one big upgrade.

Food and cargo

  • There are 4 crates of 50 kg, each worth 25 crew-days of food. On Medium and Hard the rack holds 200 kg (Easy: 325 kg), so the supplies taken compete with the crates.
  • Food left at Alpha spoils by about 1% an hour. Rough landings crack crates. Cold freezes the food unless the heater is on or an insulation blanket is packed. If the hull is badly damaged in a storm, toxic perchlorate dust spoils the food.
  • Score: delivering 90% of the food earns "Food Guardian".

What the player learns

Dust devils can clean solar panels, as they did for Spirit and Opportunity

Mars gravity is 38% of Earth's, so the rover flies off crests

Shield the crew and fix electronics

Underground is the best shelter, but there's no sunlight for the panels

Plan for the unexpected

On harder difficulties, storms are bigger with less warning, flares are stronger and spoilage is faster.

Real data behind the numbers

  • NASA Mars Fact Sheet: gravity, sunlight, atmosphere.
  • NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD): oxygen use.
  • Hassler et al. 2014, Curiosity RAD: surface radiation.
  • NASA DONKI: the five real solar flares.
  • Real mission events: Opportunity, Spirit, Curiosity, Perseverance, MRO, Phoenix and Kilopower.
  • Canadian Space Agency: food production in space and in remote areas.

Keeping kids engaged

A blocky world to build in, inspired by Minecraft-style games

  • Mars is drawn as a 2D world of blocks: regolith, basalt, sand, ice and buried minerals. On an EVA the astronaut walks, jumps in low gravity, digs blocks and places them.
  • Building is part of the science. To survive a dust storm or flare, players wall in the rover and add a roof. A red glow shows gaps, and green means sealed. Ice blocks shield radiation twice as well, and glass roofs let sunlight reach the panels.
  • Crafting uses real ideas in the fabricator: sintered bricks made from Mars soil (like ICON's 3D-printed Mars Dune Alpha habitat), glass from sand, metal plates from iron ore, airlock doors, ladders, lamps and outpost beacons.
  • Caves to explore: ladders lead underground to rare titanium ore, opal and meteorite iron. Players bring these back to a base workshop to build bigger cargo racks (up to a long-bed rover carrying 600 kg) and better batteries.

Multiplayer

  • Players can join a lobby of up to 5 astronauts on Medium or Hard, where storms are about 20% stronger. This feature is implemented in the code (api/sync.js).
  • Players in the same lobby share one world. They see each other's rovers and astronauts as "ghosts", and blocks that one player digs or builds appear in everyone's world, so crews can share shelters and mark outposts for each other.
  • The world leaderboard ranks mission times for each difficulty, which adds friendly competition between teams and schools.
  • Note: multiplayer and the leaderboard need the game's free server storage (Redis on Vercel) to be switched on. Solo play works anywhere, even offline.

Rewards and feedback

  • 17 badges reward good habits, not just speed: Radiation Safe, Fresh Air (oxygen never below 25%), Iron Hull, Food Guardian, Master Builder (ride out a storm in your own shelter), Cave Explorer, Space Weather Ready, and "Seven Minutes of Terror" for a perfect landing.
  • Real-data moments: Mission Control messages and event cards connect each in-game event to a real mission ("In 2018 a planet-wide dust storm silenced Opportunity…").
  • Short sessions, replayable: each drive takes minutes, the first trip follows a set route so players can learn it, and later trips bring random storms and flares.
  • Original chiptune music is generated in the browser, with an option for players to add their own songs.
  • Easy to access: it is one web page that needs no install. It works on computers with a keyboard and mouse, and on phones and tablets with on-screen buttons.

What players come away with

  • Systems thinking: power, air, radiation, communication and mass are linked, and improving one costs another.
  • Planning with real numbers: "How many hours of oxygen do I need for a 2.5-hour drive with a possible storm?"
  • Risk management: deciding when to shelter, when to push on and when to spend oxygen on a repair.
  • Engineering and building: designing a rover under a mass limit, and building shelters from local materials.
  • Teamwork: sharing a world and helping other crews in multiplayer.
